# Tiered Support

`customer_support.model.tiered_support` · model · parent `—`

> L1 generalists, L2 product specialists, L3 engineering-adjacent, and a written criterion for crossing each boundary. What the structure buys is specialisation and, above everything else, a shield: L3 is the scarcest capacity in the company and the ladder exists so that volume never reaches it. That benefit is real and it is fragile — the moment L1 is under-skilled the shield leaks upward, and the org is left carrying every cost of the model with none of the protection it was built for. . What it pays is handoffs. Each tier is its own queue with its own backlog and its own arrival order, so a ticket "escalated to our specialists" frequently joins the back of a slower line: the customer was told it sped up at the exact moment it slowed down. The SLA clock does not restart at a tier boundary but the queue position does, and tier queues sorted by their own arrival time rather than by time remaining are the most common structural cause of breach in this model. The customer pays in repetition — they re-describe the problem to each new stranger — and it is characteristically the second handoff, not the elapsed hours, where their patience ends. . The permanent management problem is the L1 metric, and it does not have a clean answer. Measure L1 on resolution rate and they hoard tickets they cannot solve, because escalating counts against them. Measure them on speed or on volume cleared and they escalate prematurely to clear their board. Both failures saturate L2, both are invisible in an org-level dashboard that only shows aggregate resolution time, and every tiered org oscillates between them. The only stable L1 target is correct disposition — did this ticket end up in the right place, at the right time, with the right context — which is a quality judgement and therefore expensive to measure, which is why so few orgs do it. . Worth knowing before switching a branch: this is the structure commercial contracts were written against. "Escalated to tier two within two hours" has a referent here and none in a flat or swarming org, so a tiered org can satisfy clauses its swarming successor structurally cannot. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a pooled or swarming team: that whoever answers can finish it, and can therefore promise. In a tiered org the first responder frequently does not yet know whether the answer is theirs, and a commitment made at L1 is delivered — or missed — by an L3 who never saw it being made. The second carry-over error is treating the assignee as the relationship owner. After two transfers the ticket has an owner and the customer does not, which is precisely when they start chasing, and the chase arrives at L1 who can no longer answer it.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | unchanged by the model — tiering describes who answers, and the customer's only direct experience of it is being passed on |
| typical_resolution_hours | 18 |
| volume_shape | moderate to high volume with a long difficulty tail; the tail is the entire reason the ladder exists and the middle is where it costs |
| staffing_model | L1 generalists, L2 product specialists, L3 engineering-adjacent, with a written skill-boundary criterion between each level |
| coverage | wide at L1, thin and business-hours at L2 and L3 — the ladder narrows exactly as it deepens, so an out-of-hours L3 problem waits regardless of severity |
| automation_level | moderate; deflection and macros sit at and in front of L1, and their real job is protecting L2 capacity rather than saving L1 time |
| primary_channels | `ticket_portal`, `email`, `phone`, `chat` |
| notes | Tier boundaries must be written as SKILL boundaries, never as effort boundaries. "L1 tries for fifteen minutes and then escalates" is the single most common way the criterion is written and it produces a permanent queue of half-diagnosed tickets at L2 — the timer guarantees the handoff happens at whatever point the diagnosis had reached, which is unrelated to whether anything useful was established. The correct criterion names what L1 is equipped to conclude, and the corollary is that changing L1's training changes the boundary.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `assignee_ref`, `queue_ref`, `team`, `assignment_count`, `is_escalated`


> `assignment_count` is this model's own diagnostic and it is not a workflow statistic: it is the number of times the customer has been re-introduced to a stranger. One is the design. Two is where satisfaction characteristically falls away. A ticket sitting at four has a handoff problem rather than a difficulty problem, and reading it as a hard ticket sends it to a fifth person. `team` and `queue_ref` are both required because the tier that owns the queue and the team currently holding the work diverge during a transfer, and that divergence window is where tickets go missing.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `direction`, `level`, `receiving_owner_ref`, `context_handed_over`, `handoff_note`, `diagnosis_repeats`


> `direction` is the field that separates the two things the word "escalation" means in a tiered org: up a tier, which is a skill transfer and a routine event, and up a management line, which is a relationship event and is not routine at all. They arrive through the same word, land in the same field in most tooling, and want opposite responses — one needs an engineer, the other needs an apology and an owner. `diagnosis_repeats` is the customer-side cost made countable: it records how many times the same question has been asked of them, which is the number they will quote when they finally complain.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `clock_state`, `elapsed_minutes`, `remaining_minutes`


> The clock belongs to the ticket and the backlog belongs to the tier, and nothing in the default tooling reconciles the two. A ticket entering L2 carries a clock that is already two-thirds spent and takes a queue position that knows nothing about it. Sorting each tier's queue by remaining time rather than by arrival into that tier is the one change that removes most breaches in this model, and it is unpopular at L2 because it makes their queue order look arbitrary from the inside.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `due_at`, `action`


> The promise is made at the tier that cannot keep it. L1 says "an engineer will come back to you today" because that is what the customer needs to hear, and the delivery belongs to someone who never saw the sentence. A commitment in this branch therefore has to survive the transfer as an attribute of the ticket rather than of the agent — otherwise every handoff silently voids every outstanding promise, and the customer's experience of the ladder is that people stop keeping their word as it goes up.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `audience`, `article_type`, `owner_ref`


> In a tiered org the majority of the knowledge base is written for the tier below, not for the customer, and conflating the two audiences produces articles that serve neither. An L2 who resolves a ticket without writing the L1-executable version has bought themselves the identical ticket next month, at their own desk — which is the mechanism by which a tiered org's senior capacity gets consumed by problems it has already solved.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `technical_fluency`, `prior_escalation_count`


> Fluency is a routing input here in a way it is not elsewhere: a requester who has already run the L1 diagnostics themselves and says so should not be made to run them again, and the standard tiered intake makes them do exactly that. It is the single fastest way to convert a competent, calm customer into an escalation.

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> Operating-structure branch, and the default one — most support orgs are tiered without ever having decided to be, because the structure is what a growing queue produces on its own when the first specialist is hired. That is why this file spends its length on costs rather than on benefits: the benefits are why it was adopted, the costs are what nobody wrote down. Read against swarming_support, which pays the opposite price for the opposite benefit.
